entries.title: Smoky Skies Are Coming Back
entries.summary: We should really have a better way of knowing when it’s safe to go outside.
entries.content:
We should really have a better way of knowing when it’s safe to go outside.

The air is bad this summer. Really, it’s historically disgusting. Smoke from wildfires has gusted over people’s homes, spreading haze and yellowing the sky. Last week, four midwestern cities—Chicago, Detroit, Milwaukee, and Toledo—reached the highest levels of particulate pollution they’ve recorded in two decades. For more than 100 million Americans across at least 20 states, the weather was grim: fumy with a chance of scattered lung conditions.

The air was bad like this two years ago, during that summer’s set of conflagrations—and let’s not forget the epic plumes of 2021, which turned the full moon over New York City a ghastly shade of red. Welcome to the new America: the land of burning throats.

In some respects, our skies have gotten cleaner in the past few decades; average levels of fine particulate matter have been cut nearly in half since 2000. But wildfires have been getting bigger and more frequent, and sending off plumes of air pollution that come and go in noxious episodes. The climate trend goes in only one direction, so this will be our future. That means we’ll need to have a better sense of when it’s safe to be outside, when it’s time to skip our morning stroll, and when we ought to keep our children home from camp. We’ll need to learn to live with smoke.

Enter the air-quality index: a weather metric for the age of wildfires. Perhaps you have never heard of the AQI or noticed it only last week, in news reports and weather-app alerts, when the smoke was getting thick. Chances are that you’ll be looking at it quite a bit in years ahead. But the AQI’s color-coded warnings, which run from wary orange (“unhealthy for sensitive groups”) to Grim Reaper maroon (“hazardous”), are useful only in the broadest sense: They may call attention to the risks of breathing smoke and remind you to be careful. As a tool, the AQI is inconsistent overall—its forecasts can be slow and imprecise, and its particulars don’t always have a bearing on direct experience. If wildfire events will get only more common, then this lousy measure must be fixed.

Globally, there’s no agreement on what constitutes unhealthy air—and no standard index of air quality. America’s version of the AQI was first created 50 years ago, as a way to standardize recording and reporting of pollutants and to clarify communications to the public. The system works like this: The concentrations of five pollutants—particulate matter, ozone, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, and carbon monoxide—are measured throughout the day at thousands of monitoring stations across the country; the readings are then combined and measured against safety thresholds that are based on regulatory limits. The AQI score is assigned such that a value of 100—which is supposed to mark the line between safe conditions and potential hazards—corresponds to standards set by the federal government.

Even just that fact can be a problem, Kevin Cromar, the director of the Health, Environment, and Policy program at NYU’s Marron Institute of Urban Management, told me. The regulatory limits for pollutants are, in theory, a reflection of those pollutants’ risk to human health. But that connection may be indirect, and the thresholds certainly aren’t calibrated perfectly for use by members of the public, who might use the AQI to figure out whether it would be safe to take a walk.

Another problem stems from the distribution of air-pollution sensors around the country. Where these are abundant, as in major cities, the reliability of any given reading might be high. But other parts of the country are more like sensor deserts, where AQI scores are interpolated from readings made in far-off places, and precision is reduced. The variation in uncertainty is not communicated to the public. AQI reports tend to look the same—a single number—no matter where you are.

In some countries, air-quality scores are calibrated to reflect whatever mix of pollutants happens to be airborne on any given day. The United States is more single-minded: It focuses only on whichever pollutant has a concentration that most exceeds the standards, and disregards the rest. If, say, there was enough nitrogen dioxide on Monday for an AQI score of 105 and enough ozone for a score of 103, our air-quality reports would give only the former number: 105. Now imagine that on Tuesday, the nitrogen dioxide held at 105, while ozone levels dropped to 30. The resulting AQI report would look the same as it had the day before—again, 105—even if the air felt much better in the lungs of a person with asthma. Given this design, Cromar said, the meaning of the index may even be inverted from time to time, with a higher AQI corresponding to a lower risk of health effects.

This sort of issue would be easy to ignore under conditions like last week’s, when a single factor—particulate matter from wildfire smoke—dominated readings. But the mixed-pollutant problem points to a deeper issue with AQI: It can be hard to know what the numbers really mean. AQI reporting isn’t standardized across weather apps and news reports. In some places, you might see the measure as a total average for the day; in others, you’ll get a moving average (known officially as NowCast) that tries to show you how air quality is changing by the hour; still others, such as the basic weather app on my Google phone, offer up a mysterious hybrid of the two. Cromar told me that even people in his field—which is to say, the most sophisticated consumers of this sort of information—may be flummoxed by the range of AQI reports. “It’s a mess,” he said. “There’s just a lot of different information out there, and it’s unreasonable to expect the public to somehow make sense of all that.”

Then there’s the fact that different people may react in very different ways to the same concentrations of particulate matter, or the same readings on the index. In a smokier era, we’ll each have to learn for ourselves how the AQI numbers that show up on our phone relate to our sensations and experience. Cromar said that we’ll have to form new types of weather intuitions: Oh, the AQI is 135; I know what that feels like—I’ll put off my shopping ’til tomorrow.

Or maybe we could just get rid of AQI completely and have our apps provide us with raw measurements instead: a daily digest of pollutant concentrations, laid out in micrograms per cubic meter. At first, these data would be cryptic—who besides the biggest air-pollution nerd would know the difference between 35 μg/m3 of particulate matter (yellow-level risk, per the AQI) and 60 μg/m3 (red-level risk)? But then again, none of us was born with the understanding that 35 degrees Fahrenheit is cold and 60 degrees is pretty nice. I also had to learn, at some point in my adult life, that 35 percent relative humidity is very dry for where I live, whereas 60 is about average. This is true for every number in our weather apps: the daily highs and lows, the chance of rain, the UV scores, the pollen counts. You have to gain a feel for what they mean.

We’ve already formed internal models when it comes to measured temperatures, wind-chill factors, and the heat index. Now the weather’s turning, and it’s time to do the same for smoke.

entries.title: Too Scared for Sex
entries.summary: The therapist Esther Perel has a theory about America’s eroticism shortage.
entries.content:
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.

A little more than 20 years ago, Esther Perel was not yet an author or a podcast host. She was definitely not a household name. She was simply a psychotherapist with an observation: Many of her clients were in loving, supportive romantic relationships—and they weren’t having good sex, or any at all. At the time, the prevailing wisdom among psychologists was that a couple’s sex life was a reflection of their bond. Cultivate closeness, the thinking went, and you will feel safe to explore and to shed inhibitions. But Perel kept noticing the opposite: Emotional intimacy and desire seemed often to be at odds.

That idea is fairly commonplace now—but that’s because Perel helped popularize it. In her 2006 book, Mating in Captivity, she described a kind of Greek tragedy that can thwart couples. Two people in heady early love, fearing uncertainty and aloneness, rush to get closer. But in doing so, they smother the spark of mystery that made the other person so desirable in the first place. Her book was a massive best seller, translated into more than 30 languages. Now she speaks in sold-out concert venues. Earlier this summer, The Invite, a film based partly on Mating’s ideas, was released in theaters. (Olivia Wilde, the director and star, is a stan.) In May, when I went to an event Perel hosted in New York City, a line of attendees young and old stretched down the block, several carrying bags with one of her catchphrases: If you’re too busy for sex, you’re too busy.

Perel has covered plenty of other subjects over the years. Still, her initial thesis has only gained relevance. Two decades after the book’s release, American culture is in a bit of a sensual drought—and people want to know why. According to some data, the average married couple have less sex now. Young adults are entering partnerships later and less often, and a striking number of them don’t even want to see sex on TV.

But Perel has said she doesn’t want to focus on statistics. The endless measurement of sex—how often people are having it, with how many partners, starting at what age—strikes her as part of the problem: It’s a distinctly unsexy and terribly narrow way to understand desire. She’s interested, instead, in eroticism. Perel’s “erotic” can entail sex, but it doesn’t have to. It’s a state one enters into when they’re playful, intrigued, open to the unknown. And because it means venturing away from security, it always involves some risk.

Perhaps the “sex recession,” then, is merely a symptom of something bigger: an eroticism shortage, resulting from a great discomfort with uncertainty. If so, the stakes would be much higher than they were in 2006. It would mean that people aren’t just falling out of lust with their partner but struggling to connect, to feel deeply, and to be present for their own life. “Today, the question is not so much How do you sustain desire in the long haul,” Perel told me, “but How do we ignite it in the first place?”

Eroticism, as Perel sees it, can begin only when one has achieved a baseline sense of safety. She has said she came to this understanding in part because of her husband’s career as a psychologist working with torture survivors. Once, she asked him how he knows when someone has truly come back—when they’ve gone from being not dead to alive. He told her it’s when they can be creative. In order to explore, to be open to new ideas and experiences—all core to eroticism, in Perel’s view—people have to feel stable enough to let their guard down. They have to unclench.

One doesn’t need to be a torture survivor to be in the habit of clenching: scanning for danger rather than being silly or raunchy or mischievous. “If you are in a state of vigilance,” Perel said, “you cannot be playful.”

Americans do seem more vigilant than playful these days. According to one 2025 poll from Marquette University Law School, 66 percent of 18-to-29-year olds and 60 percent of 30-to-44-year olds agreed that “most people can’t be trusted.” Rates of avoidant attachment style—the tendency to keep distant, essentially—have been rising. Political priorities have become dominated by a yearning for security: protection against financial instability, crime, replacement. And politicians are rushing to acknowledge (or exploit) those fears. These are not the conditions in which eroticism thrives.

The result is that while readers have continued lapping up Mating in Captivity, Americans have broadly become worse at taking Perel’s advice. The central premise of the book is that partners can keep the erotic alive by accepting that they will never know each other completely. But the average couple have arguably become more intertwined. For a recent story on Americans’ particularly intense disdain for infidelity, I spoke with a sociologist who said that many people are disturbed by the idea that their partner could have needs and fantasies they don’t know about. Cheating is so despised, she argued, because it’s a reminder that no matter how much of yourself you share and how close you are to your partner, you’ll never be inside their mind.

The fear of an unrecognizable partner is, at the moment, a notable obsession of popular culture. Take Strangers, Belle Burden’s mega-best-selling memoir about being left by her husband—suddenly, with no explanation. Over the course of the book, she replays their relationship in her head, searching for clues; she wonders whether something in his childhood set this in motion. When his previous behavior doesn’t leave a bread-crumb trail straight to his present actions, Burden makes it sound as creepy as if she’d been stuck in the house with her husband’s evil twin. On the Netflix horror series Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen, the primary source of dread is not the jump scares or the protagonist’s strange in-laws but the looming question of whether her fiancé isn’t who she thought he was. And in the April film The Drama, a man named Charlie (played by Robert Pattinson) learns something about his fiancée, Emma (Zendaya), that upends his understanding of her right before their wedding. Again and again he rewrites his vows, desperately searching for a cohesive story about his relationship.

You might think that in the past two decades, Americans would’ve grown accustomed to uncertainty. But Perel believes that many people are struggling to cope with that precarity. Why learn how, when you can use Google Maps to see exactly how delayed your train is, or ask ChatGPT to give you a breakdown of anything you don’t immediately understand? In a superficial sense, the world is more graspable and predictable than ever. Sometimes, though, that can make a person more afraid of ambiguity, more attached to the fiction that we can ever know what’s around the corner—or in our partner’s head.

On top of that, Perel said, the kinds of communities and rituals people traditionally relied on when facing enigma and loss aren’t so common anymore. Fewer Americans are looking to religion to answer the big questions—how to live, what happens after death, why bad things happen to good people—or to let them wrestle with these issues communally. Fewer socialize regularly with their neighbors. The average family size keeps shrinking. A lot of people don’t know where else to look for certainty but their partner. So they cling for dear life.

An aversion to the unknown isn’t a problem just for couples; it’s a problem for people without partners too, and for the culture at large. Single people are approaching first dates as if they’re interviews, ready to review the candidate, on the lookout for red flags. Or they’re not dating at all, sometimes even when they want sex or love. In my own reporting on romance, I hear from a lot of people on the defense against hurt feelings or wasted time. The weight of the world—the dismal news alerts, the rent bills, the doomscrolling—isn’t putting them in the mood for lighthearted banter or seductive dancing or organic inquisitiveness.

Americans seem to be losing their taste for pleasure, sexual or not. In growing numbers, they’re short-circuiting their appetites with GLP-1s. They’re covering their homes in beige, following influencers who quietly tidy, and half-heartedly streaming mild comedies while they scroll. “The culture of these years,” my colleague Spencer Kornhaber wrote recently, “will be remembered for lots of things that dulled and distracted the senses: easygoing country music, friendly AI chatbots, ketamine nasal sprays.” And dulled senses are an enemy to eroticism.

Perel believes that part of the problem is that people think they’re meant to heal first—to overcome burnout, to process trauma, to somehow refresh themselves until they’re shiny and new, ready for life to get more fun and more dynamic. But if you open the door to the uncertain and unpredictable, you let in suffering along with joy. The erotic isn’t what comes after pain; it’s a way of living with it.

Maybe that’s the path forward for couples and single people alike: to lean into the precarity, not because it’s easier or more pleasant but because they’re interested in where that will lead. Perel tells partners that they don’t need to try creating distance or adding novelty to their relationships; all they need to do is accept that it already exists. In fact, they should revel in the fact that they’ll always have more to discover about each other. (A lot of couples go out for dinner with friends and have fascinating, deep conversations, she told me—and then as soon as they’re alone again, “they switch to talking about who’s going to the ball game tomorrow.”) And what if single people started treating dates as adventures—opportunities to get to know someone new and do something different? Her advice, regardless of relationship status, is essentially this: Never give yourself over to numbness.

In The Invite, Olivia Wilde’s film, two couples have a dinner party. One of those pairs seems electric with chemistry and presence; they laugh, touch each other with affection, speak aloud the observations that might have been politely contained. The other pair has had the life “seeped out of them,” as Perel put it to me. They’re on autopilot. They’re a little like a lot of people, in an age of blunted pleasure. The question of the film is whether the vitality of that first couple might wake them up.

Spoiler alert: The movie is ambiguous on that point. But it does contain a hopeful note—much like The Drama, actually. Both films show their stunted couples attempting to start over, reenacting the beginning of their relationship, when everything was terrifyingly and beautifully undetermined. “I’m Emma,” Zendaya’s character says, and Charlie returns her handshake across the table. The viewer can only guess whether they’ll be brave enough to remain curious.

This article originally attributed polling on American trust to the Badger Institute. In fact, Marquette University Law School conducted the survey.

entries.title: Why So Much Millennial Fiction Is Boring
entries.summary: The generation’s novels tend to focus on the flatness of modern life—but alienation doesn’t have to be dull.
entries.content:
The generation’s novels tend to focus on the flatness of modern life—but alienation doesn’t have to be dull.

Perhaps every generation believes that it is unsuited to its own era. As an elder Millennial, I can’t help but see how perfectly primed my cohort was for feelings of inadequacy and distress. Raised on the standard American diet of promise and progress, many in my micro-generation arrived in high school just in time for the Columbine shootings to undermine our sense of safety. As many of us entered the age of military fitness, the Twin Towers fell and the United States embarked on a forever war. The Great Recession greeted our arrival into the job market, and coronavirus-pandemic lockdowns coincided with the years when a lot of us were becoming parents. Now our early middle age is marked by inflation, environmental chaos, and AI’s potentially existential threat to job stability. Even if most generations complain about discontent, mine may have a particularly strong case for it.

What’s a fiction writer to do with all of that joylessness? Plenty of authors in generations past made it their subject. Anna Karenina, Emma Bovary, and Tess Durbeyfield didn’t lead lives of unmitigated bliss. But contemporary fiction has a particular task: to explain and make interesting the deep disaffection of this era. It isn’t sadness, exactly, that lurks inside the hearts of Millennials and their similarly cursed younger siblings Gen Z, but something closer to lack—of security, of certainty, of sensual engagement with the world. The novelist who wants to write about how young people (barely) get by in the world today has to explain why all of this overwhelm often translates into paralysis—without boring readers to distraction.

Like its cousin the internet novel, the novel of alienation needs a stylistic foil to make it sing. Methodically charting the flatness of ennui won’t get you very far; when your readers feel as listless as your characters do, they’re likely to reach for their phone in search of dopamine hits. Instead, you have to jolt your audience into an uneasy kinship.

In I Want You to Be Happy, Jem Calder’s first novel, the author fails at this delicate task, and not spectacularly but anemically. His premise is simple: Chuck, a 35-year-old recently unengaged copywriter, meets the 23-year-old Joey, a barista with no better career prospects in view. For a few months, they casually date—a classic “situationship,” dogged on both sides by ambivalence and occasional apathy. Eventually, the relationship comes to an impasse, and each has to decide whether it’s worth their energy to carry on.

But energy is scarce in Calder’s writing. Chuck and Joey have the kind of colorless sex that Calder describes in a monotone: “He asked her the universal male sex-act-recipient questions.” The couple also have very little to say to each other in between beddings. One date features “some discussion comparing alcohol and coffee,” and during a long weekend in the country, among their most intimate remarks is: “The showers here are good.”

Both partners are flailing: Chuck is put on a performance-improvement plan at his firm for poor productivity and frequent hangovers, and Joey cannot afford to buy a cocktail or live anywhere better than the squalid bedroom that she rents in a shared house. But they regard their positions with little emotion beyond self-pity. In fact, that’s how they look at all of life. Neither has any hobbies or intellectual pursuits: Nobody so much as waters a plant or visits a museum. Both claim that they want to be a writer, and these dreams generate some intriguing tension, but readers rarely get a glimpse of what they produce. Joey reads two books that we know of, a work of poetry she admires for reasons that she does not explain and another described only as “boring.” Although I Want You to Be Happy is set in present-day London, no one probes the sorry state of the post-Brexit British government, except to comment vaguely that life is too expensive and friends are leaving the city. Most important, no one displays even a wisp of curiosity. The inner lives of Chuck and Joey are as untextured as the phone screens they tap incessantly.

Curiosity, perhaps more than any other characteristic, is what pulls a reader along for a fictional ride. A character may simply want to find out how their new neighbor is getting along (The Great Gatsby), or whether they’ve married the right person (Middlemarch), or whether they’ll catch the damn whale (you know the one). But along the way, a single musing can turn into many more, like branching rows of dominoes setting off new lines of inquiry about the world. Even in novels centered on Millennial inaction or stasis, such as Pond, by Claire-Louise Bennett, a kind of attentiveness is necessary to advance beyond rhetorical water-treading.

Other writers have successfully captured the malaise afflicting the under-45 crowd and offered nutrient-dense characters. In her clever 2021 debut novel, Three Rooms, the British writer Jo Hamya uses social realism to chronicle the downward mobility of a bright young thing, an Oxford postdoc researcher who moves from university-adjacent housing to an acquaintance’s couch and then to her childhood bedroom, her future dimming a little bit more with each domestic downgrade. By setting the action in 2018 and 2019, during the prolonged debacle of Brexit negotiations, Hamya links the degradation of the college degree to the stagnation—in the government, the economy, the culture—that has impeded progress for an entire generation.

Hilary Leichter’s 2023 novel, Terrace Story, is similarly concerned with the indignities of the housing market, but this novelist employs a different artistic lever to keep the wheels turning: She uses dark fantasy to set our world in grim relief. A magical terrace appears inside the apartment of a young family struggling to pay the rent, offering them a chance to see how the other half lives. But it also cleaves the family apart, sending them spinning toward strange futures on a warped planet Earth. Despite these complications, Terrace Story delivers a brilliant contemporary fable that chronicles how young people stuck in the saddest timeline can still make meaning.

Not every successful novel of alienation turns on financial deprivation. In fact, the central problem in Vincenzo Latronico’s Perfection, which dispenses with dialogue entirely in depicting two vacant creative professionals, is the comfort and style of their apartment. Scandinavian armchairs and monstera houseplants are all that this couple have: The accumulation of purely superficial identity markers, which they offer up online as proof of some mythical, unrealized happiness, leaves them weary and adrift. Using hyper-specific examples (Kraftwerk LPs, the German migrant crisis of 2015 and 2016), Latronico creates a book that functions as a time capsule—one that beautifully realizes his characters’ disenchantment, precisely imagining what it’s like to become trapped by an artificial, digital version of oneself.

Some recent satires fail to reach the same heights of ingenuity, but they still have the consolations of humor. In her 2021 novel, Fake Accounts, Lauren Oyler’s snappy bons mots thoughtfully ridicule our contemporary culture of disdain even as they indulge in it to a wearying degree. And in the slightly exasperating Banal Nightmare, from 2024, Halle Butler has a knack for capturing the ludicrous way that therapy-speak has turned a generation of wobbly neurotics from patients into self-ordained shrinks.

Calder, however, lacks even a hint of humor. I Want You to Be Happy has the ambience of a dentist’s waiting room: lots of barely stifled dread accompanied by relentless scrolling. Calder may have mistaken writing about boredom for writing boredom. His prose about phone usage emphasizes physical acts (“He gaze-unlocked his phone, thumbed to his conversation with Joey, absently flexed his free hand open and closed beside the screen, then relocked his device”) rather than immersing us in the stuff that has his characters (and so many of us) in its thrall. Cellphones are, to be fair, a problem for novelists: Their presence eliminates the face-to-face dynamism that so much classic literature uses to its advantage. (Just imagine Mr. Darcy proposing in text-speak.) But phones are also surprisingly similar to novels—both ask people to doggedly follow and emotionally invest in the lives of strangers. They are a narrative boon to any writer interested in human longing. All of which makes Calder’s book a major missed opportunity.

The novel’s lack of interest in what’s going on inside its characters’ phones becomes indistinguishable from a disinterest in what’s happening in their minds. Designing purely surface-level characters to comment on the ways that technology homogenizes culture is the kind of exercise that can create only distance between readers and characters. I want to understand alienation; I don’t want to feel alienated—and nothing more—by reading.

Young life is certainly exhausting and at times degrading and disconcerting, but is it really as boring as it is in this book? As a reasonably settled 42-year-old, I might not be the best person to ask. But as a reader, I’m certain that if novelists want to make clear just how disappointed they are in their life and the world, they’re going to have to do it with flair.
